p.x:
My sister, Mint, is 26 and she owns a small business. She makes healthy snacks from Thai fruit. At first, she worked from our kitchen. She was very hard-working: she cooked in the morning and sold her snacks at markets in the afternoon.
There were many problems. Sometimes the fruit was too expensive, and sometimes nobody bought her snacks. But Mint never gave up. She solved each problem one by one.
Then she was lucky. A big supermarket tried her snacks and loved them! Now her snacks are in fifty shops. Starting a business was a risk, but for Mint it was a big success. She says, "Anyone can succeed if they work hard."

Every year, thousands of young people in Thailand try to start their own companies. The founder of a startup usually begins with an idea to solve a problem. For example, Ploy and her co-founder Bank noticed that many students couldn't find cheap tutors, so they created an app to connect them.
First, they wrote a business plan explaining their target market, their costs and how they would make money. Then they built a simple prototype and tested it with friends. They joined a university incubator, which gave them office space and advice.
Next, they needed funding. Ploy practised her pitch many times before meeting investors. One investor bought a 15% stake in the company. Ploy also used her network to find their first customers, and some money came from crowdfunding.
The first year was hard. Rent and salaries were big overheads, and cash flow was a constant worry. When a large competitor copied their idea, it was a serious setback. Luckily, they had applied for a patent on one feature. By the end of the second year, they managed to break even. Now they plan to scale the business and expand to other countries. "You need ambition," says Ploy, "but you also need an innovative idea and a lot of patience." The company's growth has been impressive.

Popular culture loves the story of the startup founder who drops out of university, builds an app in a garage and becomes a billionaire. These success stories, featuring 'unicorns' with a valuation of over a billion dollars, have inspired a generation. Yet the reality is far less glamorous: most startups fail within five years.
One common reason is running out of money. Many startups depend on venture capital, giving investors equity in exchange for funding. This allows rapid growth, but it also creates pressure to expand quickly. A company with a high burn rate, spending far more each month than it earns, may collapse if new investment does not arrive in time.
For this reason, some founders prefer to bootstrap, funding the business from savings and early revenue. Growth may be slower, but they keep control. Advocates of the 'lean startup' approach recommend testing ideas cheaply and quickly, listening carefully to customers, and being ready to pivot when an idea is not working. Some of today's most famous companies began with a completely different product.
Programs such as accelerators, which offer training and connections in exchange for a small stake, can help. But perhaps the most important quality is perseverance. Founders who disrupt established industries rarely succeed on their first attempt; they learn from failure, adjust and try again. As one investor put it, "I don't invest in ideas. I invest in people who won't give up."
